u\), stopping is optimal in state \((n,1)\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). Together with the known bound \(p_n<1/2\) for \(n\ge4\), this yields \(\lim_{n	o\infty}p_n=1/2\).

papers.title: Galois Groups of Shifted Exponential Polynomials
papers.abstract: Consider the shifted truncations of the exponential series and their Galois groups: $$F_{n,a}(x) := \sum_{j=0}^{n}\frac{x^j}{(a+j)!}\qquad G_{n,a}:= \text{Gal}(F_{n,a}/\mathbb{Q}).$$ In this paper we prove that for every fixed integer $a>0$, the set of $n$ for which $G_{n,a}=S_n$ has natural density one, thus answering a question of Katz and Rivin.

papers.title: When Weak Submodularity Meets Matroids: How Does Standard Greedy Behave?
papers.authors: Qixin Zhang, Shi Fu, Shengminjie Chen, Chao Qian, Dacheng Tao
papers.abstract: Weakly submodular maximization finds numerous applications in machine learning, data mining and statistics. In particular, under a cardinality constraint, the standard greedy algorithm is known to attain the tight $(1-e^{-\gamma})$-approximation guarantee, where $\gamma$ denotes the submodularity ratio. However, when considering general matroid constraints, \emph{how well standard greedy can perform} has remained a longstanding open question. In this paper, we resolve this question by studying the worst-case approximation guarantee $R_{\mathrm{gr}}(\gamma,r)$ of standard forward greedy, where $r$ is the rank of matroid. Specifically, our first contribution is the following refined lower bound \begin{equation*} R_{gr}(\gamma,r)\ge \max\left\{ \frac{\gamma}{r}, \frac{\gamma^2} {B_\gamma+\sqrt{\gamma(r-1)}}, \frac{\gamma^{r+1}} {2-\gamma+\gamma^{r+1}}, \frac{\gamma^2} {14\left(B_\gamma+\sqrt{\gamma(1-\gamma)(r-1)}\right)} \right\}, \end{equation*} where $B_\gamma\triangleq2-\gamma+\gamma^2$. This lower bound not only strictly improves upon the previous guarantee of $0.4\gamma^2/(1+\sqrt{\gamma r})$, but also can recover the classical $1/2$-approximation guarantee at $\gamma=1$. Subsequently, a corresponding upper bound is established for $R_{\mathrm{gr}}(\gamma,r)$, namely, \begin{equation}\label{eq_upper_abstract} R_{gr}(\gamma,r) \le\min\left\{\frac{1}{2},20\max\left\{\frac{\gamma}{r}, \frac{\gamma^2}{B_\gamma+ \sqrt{\gamma(1-\gamma)(r-1)}}\right\}\right\}. \end{equation} For every fixed $\gamma\in(0,1)$, this equation effectively sharpens the recent $O_\gamma(1/\log(n-1))$ upper bound to $O_\gamma(r^{-1/2})$, where $n$ is the size of ground set. Putting all these results together, we eventually can obtain \[R_{gr}(\gamma,r) = \Theta\left( \max\left\{\frac{\gamma}{r}, \frac{\gamma^2} {1+\sqrt{\gamma(1-\gamma)r}}\right\} \right).\]

papers.title: Approximability of Triangulated Categories under Separable Extensions
papers.authors: Mengzhen Zhu, Yuefei Zheng, Xianhui Fu
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate the behavior of approximability under separable extensions of triangulated categories. Let $\mathcal{B}$ be an approximable triangulated category and let $\mathbf{T}=(T,\theta,\mu)$ be a smashing, stably separable exact monad on $\mathcal{B}$. Assume that the category of $\mathbf{T}$-modules $\mathbf{T}\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}_{\mathcal{B}}$ admits a canonical triangulated structure. We prove that if $T$ is right $t$-exact with respect to a $t$-structure in the preferred equivalence class of $\mathcal{B}$, then $\mathbf{T}\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}_{\mathcal{B}}$ is again an approximable triangulated category. As an application, we show that, under suitable assumptions, a smashing localization functor on an approximable triangulated category induces a recollement of approximable triangulated categories, thereby yielding a converse-type result to the gluing theorem of Burke--Neeman--Pauwels. Finally, under suitable hypotheses, we prove that separable extensions restrict naturally to the intrinsic subcategories associated with approximable triangulated categories.

papers.title: Large Deviations in Stochastic Dynamics: A Hamiltonian Perspective
papers.authors: Lorenzo Cirigliano, William D. Pi\~{n}eros, Anna Poggialini, Grant M. Rotskoff, Eric Vanden-Eijnden
papers.abstract: These lecture notes present an introduction to large deviations in stochastic dynamical systems, adapted from a lecture series given at the Les Houches school ``Large Deviations: Theory and Applications'' in July 2024. The exposition develops the theory through a unified methodology: WKB analysis of backward Kolmogorov equations, which reveals the Hamiltonian structure underlying all large deviation principles considered here. We treat three asymptotic regimes systematically. First, the small-noise limit for stochastic differential equations and the large-volume limit for Markov jump processes, where the Large Deviation Principle emerges from the Law of Large Numbers through progressively finer characterizations of fluctuations. Second, the long-time limit combined with small noise, yielding the quasipotential formalism for metastability and transition rates in both equilibrium and nonequlibrium systems. Third, the long-time limit at finite noise, connecting to spectral methods via tilted generators and enabling reduction of multiscale systems. We survey computational approaches including minimum action methods, their geometric variants for quasipotential calculations, and neural network techniques. The Schl\"{o}gl model of chemical bistability serves as a running example, illustrating both scalar and spatially extended settings. Appendices provide self-contained background on stochastic calculus and Markov jump processes.

papers.title: U torsion structure in Heegaard Floer homology
papers.abstract: We construct infinite families of Brieskorn spheres with three singular fibers for which the difference between the largest and the second largest length of $U$-torsion in their Heegaard Floer homology $HF^-$ increases to infinity as the family parameter increases. In particular, these families give a negative answer to the strong geography restriction problem by Alfieri and Binns \cite[Question 1.10]{AB24} which was added to the recent K3 list \cite[Problem 3.55, Remark(5)]{K3}. As a consequence of the results by Alfieri and Binns, these families give the examples of integer homology spheres that are neither surgery on a knot nor large surgery on links.

papers.title: Information, Estimation, and Prediction for Discrete Memoryless Channels via Poissonization
papers.abstract:
We develop information--estimation relations for an arbitrary discrete memoryless channel with finite input and output alphabets by varying the expected number of observations while keeping the channel fixed. A single hidden input is observed through a \textit{Poisson} number of conditionally independent channel uses, whose mean specifies the observation budget. The derivative of mutual information with respect to this budget equals the minimum expected relative-entropy loss for estimating the input's output distribution. The posterior average of the channel's output distributions achieves this minimum and is the Bayesian predictor for the next observation.
  When the input distribution, the channel, or both are misspecified, the relative entropy between the true and assumed observation laws is the integral of the excess prediction loss over the budget. We also extend these relations to finite-state processes taking values in the input alphabet and observed through the channel at independent Poisson sampling times. Both in the matched setting and under model mismatch, the expected prediction loss accumulated over time using past observations equals the corresponding loss using the full observation record (noncausal estimation), averaged over lower sampling rates.
  We also characterize how redundancy between two outputs selects among input distributions that achieve one-use capacity. For the coupon-collector channel, where each observation is sampled uniformly from an unknown subset, we derive the exact capacity loss of any input distribution. In particular, balanced subset families can substantially reduce the input alphabet while preserving the leading capacity terms.

papers.title: Balanced subgraph counts and quasirandomness: a proof of the Janson--S\'os conjecture
papers.authors: Guoqing Wang, Linlin Wang, Jun Yue
papers.abstract: Let $F$ be a finite simple graph with $m$ vertices and at least two edges, and let $p\in(0,1]$. We prove that a graph sequence is $p$-quasirandom if and only if the symmetrized counts of copies of $F$ across every balanced partition into $m$ classes have the asymptotics predicted by the random graph with edge probability $p$. This settles a conjecture of Janson and S\'os for all such $F$, including graphs with isolated vertices. The proof completes their graph-limit reduction by a concavity argument for a sum of fractional powers determined by the degree sequence of $F$. We also show that a symmetrized subgraph kernel of positive mean can be additive in its coordinates only when the underlying graphon is constant almost everywhere. This rigidity result yields a quasirandomness criterion for generalized restricted subgraph counts, resolving a further conjecture of Janson.

papers.title: Nonlocal Equations on Domains and Manifolds Without Symmetries
papers.abstract: In this work, we establish existence and regularity results for solutions to nonlinear nonlocal equations of the form $f(\Delta)u = U(x,u)$ and $f(\Delta_{g})u = U(x,u)$ in Euclidean and Riemannian settings, respectively. We prove existence results across three distinct geometric scenarios: bounded domains in $\mathbb{R}^n$, perturbed equations on compact Riemannian manifolds, and noncompact Cartan-Hadamard manifolds under suitable geometric curvature conditions.

papers.title: A vanishing theorem for finitely supported ideals in regular local rings
papers.abstract: A cohomological vanishing property is proved for finitely supported ideals in an arbitrary d-dimensional regular local ring. (Such vanishing implies some refined Briancon-Skoda-type results, not otherwise known in mixed characteristic.) It follows that the adjoint of a finitely supported ideal I of order a has order sup(a+1-d, 0), and that taking adjoints of finitely supported ideals commutes with taking strict transforms at infinitely near points. In particular, the adjoint of I is also finitely supported. Also: if this I is a normal ideal, then its reduction number is the least integer > d(1-1/a).

papers.title: Non-Geometric T-Duality as Higher Groupoid Bundles with Connections
papers.abstract: We propose a description of T-duality between general geometric and non-geometric backgrounds as higher groupoid bundles with connections. Our description extends the previous observation by Nikolaus and Waldorf that the topological aspects of geometric and half-geometric T-dualities can be described in terms of higher geometry. We extend their construction in two ways. First, we endow the higher geometries with adjusted connections, which allow us to discuss explicit formulas for the metric and the Kalb-Ramond field of a T-background. Second, we extend the principal 2-bundles to principal 2-groupoid bundles, which accommodate the scalar fields arising in T-dualities along two directions as well as $Q$-fluxes. Our proposals reproduce key examples from the literature. They are manifestly covariant under the full T-duality group $\mathsf{GO}(n,n;\mathbb{Z})$ and have interesting physical and mathematical implications. Eventually, we also comment on the case of T-duality in the presence of scalar fluxes.

papers.title: Certified Decisions
papers.abstract: Hypothesis tests and confidence sets are ubiquitous in empirical research, yet their connection to subsequent decision-making is often unclear. We view statistical inference as pairing recommended decisions with guarantees of their quality---or certificates---and develop a theory of certified decisions. Specifically, we attach P-certificates---upper bounds on loss that hold with probability at least $1-\alpha$---to recommended actions. We prove that it is without loss to limit attention to P-certificates generated by minimax decisions over confidence sets, or what Manski (2021) terms "as-if decisions with a set estimate." We further show that such certificates allow safe adoption decisions for ambiguity-averse downstream decision-makers. A parallel argument applies to E-certified decisions obtained from e-values in settings with unbounded loss. We illustrate this view of statistical inference through an application to economic mobility and one to AI model routing.

papers.title: Learning to Interfere in Non-Orthogonal Multiple-Access Joint Source-Channel Coding
papers.authors: Selim F. Yilmaz, Can Karamanli, Deniz Gunduz
papers.abstract: We consider multiple transmitters aiming to communicate their source signals (e.g., images) over a multiple access channel (MAC). Conventional communication systems minimize interference by orthogonally allocating resources (time and/or bandwidth) among users, which limits their capacity. We introduce a machine learning (ML)-aided wireless image transmission method that merges compression and channel coding using a multi-view autoencoder, which allows the transmitters to use all the available channel resources simultaneously, resulting in a non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) scheme. The receiver must recover all the images from the received superposed signal, while also associating each image with its transmitter. Traditional ML models deal with individual samples, whereas our model allows signals from different users to interfere in order to leverage gains from NOMA under limited bandwidth and power constraints. We introduce a progressive fine-tuning algorithm that doubles the number of users at each iteration, maintaining initial performance with orthogonalized user-specific projections, which is then improved through fine-tuning steps. Remarkably, our method supports up to 64 users with potential for further scaling, with only a 2.4% increase in the number of trainable parameters compared to a single-user model, significantly enhancing recovered image quality and outperforming existing NOMA-based methods over a wide range of datasets, metrics, and channel conditions. Our approach paves the way for more efficient and robust multi-user communication systems, leveraging innovative ML components and strategies.

papers.title: Global approximations to the error function of real argument for vectorized computation
papers.abstract: The error function of real argument can be approximated to a given uniform relative accuracy by a single closed-form expression for the whole variable range either in terms of addition, multiplication, division, and square root operations only, or also using the exponential function. Approximations to the complementary error function have also been found, including those where either only additions, multiplications, and one division, or also the exponential, are used to reach either a uniform absolute, or a uniform relative, accuracy. The coefficients have been tabulated for up to 128-bit precision. Tests of a computer code implementation using the standard single- and double-precision floating-point arithmetic show good performance and vectorizability.

papers.title: The dynamic generalized covariance measure for conditional independence testing with nonstationary time series
papers.authors: Michael Wieck-Sosa, Michel F. C. Haddad, Aaditya Ramdas
papers.abstract: Identifying relationships among stochastic processes is a core objective in many fields, such as economics. While the standard toolkit for multivariate time series analysis has many advantages, it can be difficult to capture nonlinear dynamics using linear vector autoregressive models. This difficulty has motivated the development of methods for causal discovery and variable selection for nonlinear time series, which routinely employ tests for conditional independence. In this paper, we introduce the first framework for conditional independence testing that works with a single realization of a nonstationary nonlinear process. The proposed test is designed to have power against alternatives in which the expected conditional covariance is non-zero for at least some times. We also discuss an approach for gaining power against a broader range of alternatives. The key technical ingredients of our framework are time-varying nonlinear regression, estimation of local long-run covariance matrices of products of error processes, and a distribution-uniform strong Gaussian approximation.

papers.title: Deterministic algorithms for inhomogeneous Bernoulli trials: Shapley value of network devices
papers.abstract:
Suppose that $n$ computer devices are to be connected to a network via inhomogeneous Bernoulli trials. The Shapley value of a device quantifies how much the network's value increases due to the participation of that device. Characteristic functions of such games are naturally taken as the belief function (containment function) and Choquet capacity (hitting probability) of a random set (random network of devices).
  Traditionally, the Shapley value is either calculated as the expected marginal contribution over all possible coalitions (subnetworks), which results in exponential computational complexity, or approximated by the Monte Carlo sampling technique, where the performance is highly dependent on the stochastic sampling process.
  The purpose of this study is to design deterministic algorithms for games formulated via inhomogeneous Bernoulli trials that approximate the Shapley value in linear or quadratic time, with rigorous error analysis (Sections 3 and 4). Additionally, we provide a review of relevant literature on existing calculation methods in Remark 3.1 and Appendix I.
  A further goal is to supplement Shapley's original proof by deriving the Shapley value formula using a rigorous approach based on definite integrals and combinatorial analysis. This method explicitly highlights the roles of the Binomial Theorem and the Beta function in the proof, addressing a gap in Shapley's work (Appendix II).

papers.title: Correlation of divergency: c_delta. Being different in a similar way or not
papers.authors: Johan F. Hoorn, Johnny K. W. Ho
papers.abstract: Matched sets may have unlike mean scores and spreads yet share the same way in which some scores stand apart. Mean gaps and raw-score correlations do not answer this question. Correlation of divergency, c_delta, is put forward to fill that gap. For every score in each of two equally sized, matched sets, it finds how far that score lies from every other score in its own set. It then draws these gaps into one divergence score through a power mean. The Pearson correlation between the two lists of divergence scores is c_delta, which lies between -1 and 1. A high positive value means that the same people or things stand out in both sets, no matter which way their raw scores point. A negative value means that a score far from the rest in one set tends to be matched with a score near the rest in the other, whilst a value near zero shows little linear link. As c_delta stems from within-set gaps, it is unchanged by shifts in overall level or units. It can show whether the same people feel sharply shut out in matched neighbourhood sets, whether the same bacterial strains grow oddly under two drugs, or whether the same proteins stand out in two drug-binding fingerprints. It should sit alongside means and raw-score correlations rather than take their place: c_delta does not show whether an outlier is high or low, nor why it arose. The power p sets the weight given to wide gaps. With p=1 it uses Gini distance, and with p=2 root-mean-square distance. Higher p gives more weight to the furthest gaps but cuts Kish's effective sample size. The raw scores and the choice of p must therefore be read with care.

papers.title: Level 2.5 large deviations and uncertainty relations for non-Markov self-interacting dynamics
papers.authors: Francesco Coghi, Amarjit Budhiraja, Juan P. Garrahan
papers.abstract: We address the general problem of formulating the dynamical large deviations of non-Markovian systems in a closed form. Specifically, we consider a broad class of ``self-interacting'' jump processes whose dynamics depends on the past through a functional of a state-dependent empirical observable. Exploiting a natural separation of timescales, \newnewtext{and under the corresponding mixing conditions,} we obtain the exact (so-called ``level 2.5'') large deviation joint statistics of the empirical measure over configurations and of the empirical flux of transitions. As an application of this general framework, we derive explicit general bounds on the fluctuations of trajectory observables, generalising to the non-Markovian case both thermodynamic and kinetic uncertainty relations. We illustrate our theory with simple examples, and discuss potential applications of these results.

papers.title: Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory
papers.authors: Usman Anwar, Tim Bakker, Dana Kianfar, Cristina Pinneri, Christos Louizos
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitors are LLM-based systems that analyze reasoning traces to detect when outputs may exhibit attributes of interest, such as test-hacking behavior during code generation. In this paper, we use information-theoretic analysis to show that non-zero mutual information between CoT and output is a necessary but not sufficient condition for CoT monitorability. We identify two sources of approximation error that may undermine the performance of CoT monitors in practice: information gap, which measures the extent to which the monitor can extract the information available in CoT, and elicitation error, which measures the extent to which the monitor approximates the optimal monitoring function. Empirically, we show that CoT obfuscation can arise even in the absence of any optimization pressure against CoT. We further demonstrate that the fragility of CoT monitorability can be systematically mitigated through targeted training objectives. To this end, we propose a practical, label-free objective based on mutual information between outputs and CoTs, and benchmark it against an oracle-based method that directly rewards the monitored model for CoTs that maximize monitor accuracy. Across multiple environments, we show that our objective is effective at preventing CoT obfuscation even when training against a monitor, and helps mitigate reward hacking when the task reward is imperfectly specified.

papers.title: General bounds on functionals of the lifetime under life table constraints in a joint actuarial-financial framework
papers.abstract: In life insurance, life tables provide survival probabilities at integer ages but leave the distribution of deaths within each year unspecified. This incompleteness is particularly relevant for modern insurance products such as variable annuities, whose payoffs depend jointly on lifetime uncertainty and financial market performance. The valuation of such contracts must therefore be carried out in a joint actuarial-financial framework, as their values depend not only on the full information about mortality rates but also on the interaction between mortality risk, asset dynamics and embedded guarantees. Standard approaches impose fractional-age assumptions or mortality rate models, but the resulting valuations strongly depend on these assumptions, which makes it difficult to generalize them. We hence derive upper and lower bounds of hybrid functionals of the lifetime with respect to mortality rates, which are compatible with the observed life table at integer ages and the given financial market. We derive two sets of results under distinct assumptions. In the first, we assume that each mortality trajectory is almost surely consistent with all the tabulated one-year survival probabilities. In the second, we consider a relaxed formulation that allows for deviations of the mortality rates while still being consistent in expectation with the given reference life table. These distinct yet complementary formulations characterize the worst- and best-case contract values over all mortality processes that remain compatible with the observed life-table information and the financial market. The resulting bounds provide insurers with a practical and robust risk-management tool for assessing the impact of adverse mortality dynamics on variable annuities, quantifying the uncertainty arising from incomplete life-table information, and incorporating mortality model risk into pricing decisions.

papers.title: Edge universality in Floquet sideband spectra
papers.abstract: A monochromatic voltage drive redistributes noninteracting fermions over sidebands with Bessel amplitudes. A sharp Fermi step gives the discrete Bessel source kernel, whose large amplitude edge has the Airy limit known from random matrices and propagating fronts. At zero temperature and for energy independent transmission, the deficit of the dc bias derivative of low frequency partition noise from its large bias slope is proportional to the kernel diagonal, with ac amplitude fixed. Shifting the integer threshold coordinate down by half a sideband removes the leading finite amplitude correction. For reservoirs at a common temperature, we derive the rescaled deficit's crossover through one thermal convolution per reservoir. Its leading low temperature correction is twice that of the rescaled source occupation. We specify the geometry and mode resolution needed to distinguish this signature from the full Airy point process.

papers.title: The Stepwise Informativeness Assumption: When Do Entropy Dynamics Track Reasoning Correctness in LLMs?
papers.authors: Mar Gonz\`alez I Catal\`a, Haitz S\'aez de Oc\'ariz Borde, George D. Monta\~nez, Pietro Li\`o
papers.abstract: Recent work uses entropy-based signals at multiple representation levels to study reasoning in large language models, but the field remains largely empirical. From a theoretical perspective, reductions in model uncertainty do not necessarily reflect progress toward correctness. In this work, we characterize when such alignment can be expected through the Stepwise Informativeness Assumption (SIA), which requires entropy-reducing reasoning-prefix extensions increase the probability assigned to valid answers in expectation. We show that next-token prediction can transfer answer-relevant information from training data to the model, but does not, by itself, guarantee alignment with correctness. Instead, we propose that this alignment depends on how the training regime couples reasoning traces to correct answers. Furthermore, we hypothesize observable signatures of this phenomenon and characterize its expected failure regimes. We empirically investigate how entropy dynamics relate to correctness across four reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, ARC, SVAMP, MATH) and diverse open-weight language models spanning base, instruction-tuned, and RL-trained regimes. Our results show that entropy-correctness alignment strengthens with post-training but can weaken when task difficulty exceeds model capabilities.

papers.title: Generalization and Scaling Laws for Mixture-of-Experts Transformers
papers.abstract: We develop a theory of generalization and scaling for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Transformers that cleanly separates \emph{active} per-input capacity from routing combinatorics. By conditioning on fixed routing patterns and union-bounding across them, we derive a sup-norm covering-number bound whose metric entropy scales with the active parameter budget and incurs a MoE-specific routing overhead. Combined with a standard ERM analysis for squared loss, this yields a generalization bound under a $d$-dimensional manifold data model and $C^\beta$ targets, showing that approximation and estimation trade off as in dense networks once active parameters are accounted for appropriately. We further prove a constructive approximation theorem for MoE architectures, showing that, under the approximation construction, error can decrease either by scaling active capacity or by increasing the number of experts, depending on the dominant bottleneck. From these results we derive neural scaling laws for model size, data size, and compute-optimal tradeoffs. Overall, our results provide a transparent statistical reference point for reasoning about MoE scaling, clarifying which behaviors are certified by worst-case theory and which must arise from data-dependent routing structure or optimization dynamics.

papers.title: Depth dependence of entanglement and circuit complexity in random linear optical networks
papers.authors: Laura Shou, Joseph T. Iosue, Yu-Xin Wang, Victor Galitski, Alexey V. Gorshkov
papers.abstract: We study the growth of entanglement and circuit complexity in random passive linear optical networks as a function of the circuit depth. For entanglement dynamics, we start with an initial Gaussian state with all $n$ modes equally squeezed. For random brickwork circuits, we show that entanglement, as measured by the R\'enyi-2 entropy, grows diffusively as a function of the depth, in contrast to the linear growth for random qubit brickwork circuits. In the other direction, for arbitrary circuit geometries we prove bounds on depths which ensure the average-case subsystem entanglement reaches within a constant factor of the maximum value in all subsystems, and bounds which ensure closeness of the random linear optical unitary to a Haar random unitary in $L^2$ Wasserstein distance. We also consider robust circuit complexity for random one-dimensional brickwall circuits, as measured by the minimum number of gates required in any circuit that approximately implements the linear optical unitary. Viewing this as a function of the number of modes and the circuit depth, we show the robust circuit complexity for random one-dimensional brickwall circuits scales at most diffusively in the depth with high probability, again in contrast to the linear scaling for certain random qubit circuits. The corresponding Gaussian unitary $\tilde{\mathcal U}$ for the approximate implementation retains high output fidelity $|\langle\psi|\mathcal U^\dagger \tilde{\mathcal U}|\psi\rangle|^2$ for pure states $|\psi\rangle$ with constrained expected photon-number.

papers.title: Batalin-Vilkovisky quantization with an angular twist
papers.authors: Djordje Bogdanovi\'c, Marija Dimitrijevi\'c \'Ciri\'c, Richard J. Szabo
papers.abstract: We construct cubic scalar field theory on $\lambda$-Minkowski space by combining the Batalin-Vilkovisky formalism with harmonic analysis, and produce two inequivalent noncommutative quantum field theories. The braided theory is based on a braided $L_\infty$-algebra whereby covariance dictates a spectral decomposition into cylindrical Bessel functions that diagonalise the angular Drinfel'd twist; in this theory we find the usual logarithmic ultraviolet divergences and confirm the absence of UV/IR mixing. The standard noncommutative theory is based on a classical $L_\infty$-algebra; in this theory we relate the spectral decompositions into plane wave and cylindrical harmonic eigenmodes of the Klein-Gordan operator, we verify the planar equivalence theorem, and we demonstrate a periodic form of UV/IR mixing in which non-planar correlators are generically ultraviolet finite but become non-analytic on an infinite lattice of exceptional momenta.

papers.title: Model-agnostic information transfer and fusion for classification with label noise
papers.authors: Zhu Guojun, Zhang Sanguo, Ren Mingyang
papers.abstract: Label noise presents a fundamental challenge in modern machine learning, especially when large-scale datasets are generated via automated processes. An increasingly common and important data paradigm, particularly in domains like medical imaging, involves learning from a large dataset with coarse, noisy labels supplemented by a small, expert-verified, clean dataset. This setting constitutes a typical information transfer and fusion problem. However, the significant distribution shift between the noisy and clean data violates the core overall parametric similarity assumptions of existing statistical transfer learning methods, while their reliance on parametric models is ill-suited for complex data like images. To address these limitations, this paper develops a generic model-agnostic nonparametric framework for classification with label noise, which applies to a broad class of classifiers. Our approach leverages the small clean dataset to ``purify'' the large noisy one and carefully manages the remaining ambiguous samples. This framework is underpinned by a rigorous statistical theory. Its empirical performance is demonstrated through simulations and a real-world application to medical image analysis for pneumonia diagnosis.

papers.title: Adaptive auditing of AI systems with anytime-valid guarantees
papers.authors: Siyu Zhou, Patrick Vossler, Venkatesh Sivaraman, Yifan Mai, Jean Feng
papers.abstract: A major bottleneck in characterizing the failure modes of generative AI systems is the cost and time of annotation and evaluation. Consequently, adaptive testing paradigms have gained popularity, where one opportunistically decides which cases and how many to annotate based on past results. While this framework is highly practical, its extreme flexibility makes it difficult to draw statistically rigorous conclusions, as it violates classical assumptions: the number of observations is typically limited (often 10 to 50 cases) and decisions regarding sampling and stopping are made in the midst of data collection rather than based a pre-specified rule. To characterize what statistical inferences can be drawn from highly adaptive audits, we introduce a hypothesis testing framework from two "dueling" perspectives: (i) the model's null that asserts there is no failure mode with performance below a target threshold versus (ii) the auditor's null that asserts they have a sampling strategy that will uncover a failure mode. Leveraging Safe Anytime-Valid Inference (SAVI), we formalize the auditor as conducting "testing by betting," which translates into simultaneous e-processes for testing the dueling null hypotheses. Furthermore, if the auditor is sufficiently powerful, we prove that these two hypotheses are asymptotically inverses of each other, in that passage of such an audit certifies the AI system as being globally robust. Empirically, we demonstrate that our proposed testing procedures maintain anytime-valid Type-I error control, outperform pre-specified testing methods, and can reach statistically rigorous conclusions sometimes with as few as 20 observations.

papers.title: The Sample Complexity of Multiple Change Point Identification under Bandit Feedback
papers.abstract: We study multiple change point localization under bandit feedback. An unknown piecewise-constant function on a compact interval can be queried sequentially at adaptively chosen inputs, and each query returns a noisy evaluation of the function. The goal is to identify a prescribed number of discontinuities, known as change points, within a target precision $\eta$ and confidence level $1-\delta$, while using as few samples as possible. We propose an adaptive algorithm that first detects intervals likely to contain change points and then refines their locations to precision $\eta$. We establish non-asymptotic upper bounds on its sample budget, together with corresponding lower bounds. Prior work shows that jump magnitudes alone determine the asymptotic sample complexity as $\delta\to 0$. We reveal that this picture is incomplete beyond this regime. We demonstrate, both empirically and theoretically, that for general $\delta$ and $\eta$, the complexity is jointly governed by the jumps and the relative positions of the change points.

papers.title: TNODEV: Toolbox for Neural ODE Verification
papers.authors: Abdelrahman Sayed Sayed, Pierre-Jean Meyer, Mohamed Ghazel
papers.abstract: Neural ordinary differential equations (neural ODE) gained attention in safety critical settings such as continuous-time controllers for cyber-physical systems and classifiers integrated into automated decision pipelines, raising the question whether their behavior can be formally verified. Existing tools dedicated to neural ODE provide only a single reachability call without iterative input-set refinement, limiting the precision of their verdicts to whatever one reachability call can deliver. We present TNODEV, the first formal verifier for neural ODE that integrates a falsification checker, a fast interval-based reachability backend based on continuous-time mixed monotonicity, a verification and refinement loop with three input-set splitting heuristics, and a parallel scheduler in a single end-to-end pipeline. TNODEV supports safe-set inclusion verification on pure neural ODE, neural ODE in closed loop with a neural network controller and general neural ODE (GNODE), with the safe set specified either as an interval or as the half-space intersection induced by a target classification label. We evaluate TNODEV on a range of benchmarks across safe-set inclusion and classification-robustness properties, including a direct reachability comparison against NNV 2.0 and CORA and a verification comparison against NNV 2.0 on MNIST general neural ODE classifiers.

papers.title: Reduction of Decaying Navier--Stokes Turbulence to the Quantum Pendulum
papers.abstract:
The statistics of a classical flow is a problem of quantum mechanics in loop space, and not by analogy: the loop functional of any flow is the loop-ordered exponential of the covariant derivative $\partial+\mathrm{i}v/
u$. We follow this representation from the Navier--Stokes equation to the Euler ensemble, the fixed point of the loop equation regularized by polygons with $N$ sides. Near the turning angle $ eta=\pi$ an exact operator identity, followed by an asymptotic continuum step and without a saddle-point approximation, reduces the ensemble to two quantum pendulums, the Mathieu equation; this supersedes our earlier WKB evaluation. A Monte Carlo simulation up to $N=10^5$ confirms the reduction.
  Extreme turbulence has singularities at small scales, and, as in quantum field theory, we define it by this regularization and a renormalization: the leading power of $N$ is removed, and the turbulent viscosity $	ilde
u$ remains as the single physical scale. This is a proposed definition of turbulence at infinite Reynolds number; its continuum spectrum is computed under a stated convergence condition, and its identification with physical turbulence is a hypothesis.
  The energy spectrum is a function of $\kappa=k\sqrt{	ilde
u(t+t_0)}$ that falls as $1/k$ and then as $k^{-2}$. At $\kappa=\sqrt2$ it has a weak nonanalyticity: its second derivative diverges logarithmically. At a fixed wave number the decay is therefore singular at the finite time $t_*=2/(	ilde
u k^2)-t_0$, when $t_*>0$, and the vorticity correlations oscillate in space with the period $\sqrt2\,\pi\sqrt{	ilde
u(t+t_0)}$. Of the limits of the ensemble with structure, only the pendulum limit is taken at a critical point and has a bulk dissipation that vanishes with the viscosity. A companion paper compares it with simulations and experiments.

papers.title: Learning When to Automate: Queue Control in Human-AI Service Systems
papers.authors: Giovanni Montanari, Marco Scarsini, Vianney Perchet
papers.abstract: We study a human-AI service system in which tasks arrive sequentially and are processed through a two-stage architecture: an automated chatbot followed, when necessary, by a human agent. We consider $T$ sequentially arriving tasks, each belonging to one of $K$ heterogeneous types. For each task the decision maker chooses how many resources to allocate to the chatbot, whose type-dependent success probabilities are initially unknown. Tasks not resolved by the chatbot enter type-dependent human-service queues, where they are processed by a human agent with unknown service rates. This model captures a central tradeoff in hybrid service systems: relying more on automation reduces human congestion but increases chatbot costs, while insufficient automation may overload the human agent. We propose the UCB-DPP policy, which combines Upper Confidence Bounds with Drift-Plus-Penalty control to learn the unknown parameters of the system while making queue-aware decisions. We prove that UCB-DPP achieves regret $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(K\sqrt{T})$ and guarantees mean-rate stability of the human-service queues. Simulations on synthetic instances show that the proposed policy outperforms natural baselines.

papers.title: Generalised Robust Bayes for Joint Inference of Model and Contamination
papers.authors: Masahiro Fujisawa, Masaki Adachi, Takuo Matsubara
papers.abstract: Robust generalised Bayesian methods protect parameter inference from contamination but do not generally infer its proportion or identify individual outliers. We propose H\"older--Bayes, which applies the H\"older divergence to a scaled model to construct a joint generalised posterior over model parameters and the contamination proportion, without specifying an outlier distribution. Each posterior draw flags a corresponding number of observations least compatible with the fitted model; averaging selections propagates joint uncertainty to outlier-detection scores. Under fixed, non-negligible contamination, we establish uniform boundedness of the posterior influence function, a finite-sample $n^{-1/2}$ bound on posterior-averaged excess risk, and a Bernstein--von Mises theorem. Tail overlap between the outlier distribution and the fitted model controls the population risk minimiser's bias and the associated change in limiting posterior covariance. Interpreting the posterior temperature as an affine volume scaling yields a closed-form, data-driven choice. Simulations and real-data experiments demonstrate robust estimation, contamination-proportion recovery, and posterior-guided data cleaning.

papers.title: Centripetal Structure under Alienation-Based Abstention
papers.abstract: Alienation-based abstention makes participation endogenous because the platforms chosen by parties determine who votes. We study how voter tolerance affects the existence, location, and persistence of pure-strategy equilibria in two versions of a two-party spatial model. In the first, office-seeking parties maximize voter plurality; in the second, they care about the policy implemented. We characterize all office-seeking equilibria through a condition called window dominance, which gives a distributional characterisation of profitable deviations both near to and far from a party's platform. For general continuous voter distributions, pure strategy equilibrium in the office seeking game may fail to exist, may be non-unique, and may appear and disappear as tolerance increases. To resolve this, we identify a centripetal structure in the set of positions that can not lose to each rival. When this structure holds, a single anchor defeats every other platform and determines the unique office-seeking equilibrium. The classical Downs and Llavador results are special cases. We show that this structure persists at all larger tolerance radii once it holds at a radius of at least half the policy space and at least twice the median's distance from the center. The centripetal structure emerges before full participation for all voter distributions. Finally, the same structure yields a complete classification of equilibrium when parties care about the policy implemented rather than electoral victory alone.

papers.title: Exact quantum circuits for a lattice Boltzmann realization of the Dirac equation
papers.authors: Nilesh Sawant, Ethan Young, Kevin Patrick Griffin, Michael Martin
papers.abstract: The quantum lattice Boltzmann scheme of Succi and Dellar advances a four-component Dirac spinor on a lattice by a fixed sequence of local, exactly norm-preserving operations: a basis rotation, a collision, a streaming shift, and the inverse rotation. While this correspondence has been noted qualitatively, it has remained unclear whether it can be realized exactly and unitarily as a gate-model quantum circuit. This unitarity is a structural property of the scheme, which should, in principle, enable an operator-by-operator port onto quantum hardware. We give a gate-level construction of every operation of the three-dimensional Dirac QLB scheme: the fixed rotation gates, the collision gate, the streaming shift as a controlled increment on a position register, the position-dependent potential as a phase oracle, and periodic and reflecting boundary conditions as unitary circuits. Together, these constructions provide the first complete demonstration that the scheme is exactly representable in the gate model without any approximation beyond the classical method itself. We then compose them into single-axis, two- and three-dimensional time steps. On a state-vector emulator the resulting circuits reproduce the classical QLB solver to machine precision, thus verifying our quantum implementation. Our aim is representability and correctness rather than computational speedup; questions of state preparation, asymptotic cost, and hardware noise are identified as open avenues for future work. Appendices restore physical units, derive the scheme's Zitterbewegung in closed form and compare it with a trapped-ion simulation, and execute a reduced two-site instance on a Rigetti superconducting processor, where choosing the qubits from the live calibration lowers the state-preparation error. All operators, circuits, and figures are reproducible from the open-source quantumKineticMethods library.

papers.title: Optimal concentration and gradient sensing by perfect monitors
papers.abstract: Cells often estimate chemical concentrations from only a few diffusing molecules, whose stochastic motion limits sensing precision. We consider a perfect monitoring instrument that records the instantaneous molecular density throughout a finite region without perturbing the concentration field or distinguishing molecular identities. The standard Berg-Purcell estimator weights all positions uniformly. Here we derive the optimal spatial weighting within a large class of unbiased estimators for both concentration and gradient sensing. Variance minimization maps to an electrostatic problem. Surprisingly, although the instrument monitors the entire volume, the optimal estimator assigns all weight to its boundary, reducing the uncertainty in both concentration and gradient sensing. We extend the results to arbitrary geometries and spatial dimensions.

papers.title: A minimum witness for the 3/2 configuration-linear-program gap in two-weight graph balancing, unique at its size
papers.abstract: Restricted assignment minimizes makespan, the busiest machine's load, when each job has one size and a set of allowed machines. Its tightest studied relaxation is the configuration linear program, which fractionally gives each machine whole job sets that fit. Its integrality gap, the worst-case ratio of integral optimum to relaxation value, is open in general. On two-weight graph balancing (sizes 1 and 2, each job allowed on at most two machines) the gap is known: Jansen, Land, and Maack (2016) give both bounds. Their Table 1 instance attains 3/2, and their Corollary 11 bound of 2-s/b for sizes s < b matches it at {1,2}. We ask how small such an instance, a witness, can be. We give a six-job witness I* on the complete graph on four machines: unit jobs form a cycle through all four, and two weight-2 jobs take the remaining edges. I* has integral optimum 3 against relaxation value 2, one job fewer than the smallest earlier witness of this class. We prove I* minimum and unique at its size, on any number of machines: no instance with at most five jobs reaches gap 3/2, and at six jobs I* is the only witness, up to relabeling machines and adding unusable machines. At seven jobs uniqueness fails: we classify all thirteen witnesses, including the Jansen-Land-Maack instance. Eight jobs give 154, nine 1,662. At least four machines are necessary. Kartak et al. (2015) classified the extremal non-round-up instances of the same relaxation in one-dimensional cutting stock for small demand; the Discussion relates them. Recognizing witnesses at relaxation value 2, shared by all ours, is coNP-complete, so no min-max characterization with polynomially checkable conditions exists unless NP = coNP. Every feasibility decision behind the exhaustive claims was made twice, in floating-point and exact rational arithmetic, with identical results. We accept the pipeline's negatives only after it rediscovers I*.

papers.title: The 11/6 supremum of the Wang-Sitters rounding scheme for graph balancing
papers.authors: Adam Y. Shavit (Hunter College,The Graduate Center, CUNY)
papers.abstract: Wang and Sitters' 11/6-approximation for graph balancing (each job allowed on at most two machines) is not one algorithm but a set of permitted executions. Step 1 may return any feasible solution of the fractional relaxation. Step 3 may match remaining jobs to the rounding's slots in many ways. We determine exactly what that latitude permits: ratios arbitrarily close to 11/6, none reaching it, so 11/6 is the least constant bounding every permitted run. We then determine the worst-case guarantee, against the optimum itself, as a function of the big-job threshold beta, the fractional share at or above which Step 2 assigns a job. On Wang and Sitters' own range 1/2 < beta < 1 the guarantee is exactly max{3/2 + beta/2, 5/2 - beta}. We extend the same eligibility rule to 0 < beta <= 1/2, outside the range they state. There a big job's two shares can both reach the threshold, so Step 2 acquires a third choice. We determine it too: exactly 3/2 + (1-beta)floor(1/beta), hence unbounded as beta falls. The worst-case ratio is therefore known at every threshold in (0,1), and attained at none. Consequently 2/3 is the unique optimal threshold, and the guarantee jumps at one half and again at every threshold 1/k below it, rather than degrading smoothly. A companion note examines changes that leave the constant unchanged.

papers.title: Minimum-makespan completion and vertex selection leave the Wang-Sitters constant at 11/6
papers.authors: Adam Y. Shavit (Hunter College,The Graduate Center, CUNY)
papers.abstract: Wang and Sitters' rounding scheme for graph balancing (each job allowed on at most two machines) keeps the makespan, the busiest machine's load, within 11/6 of the optimum, and a companion note shows that no smaller constant holds. One suspected cause is Step 3's freedom to match leftover jobs to slots in any valid way. We show that removing that freedom does not improve the constant. An idealized oracle that always picks the valid matching with the smallest makespan still has worst-case constant exactly 11/6 against the optimum. Both natural 7/4 bounds for it, against the relaxation's target and against the optimum, are false. Requiring Step 1 to return a vertex (corner) of the relaxation does not help when that vertex is chosen adversarially. The loss therefore does not come from Step 3's freedom alone. We also prove a reduction confining every overload above 7/4 to two shapes, give a seven-machine instance on which the natural two-phase repair fails, and prove a strict 7/4 bound on the generalized three-path family.

papers.title: Hull Games of Induced Path Convexities in Graphs
papers.authors: Eurinardo Costa, Leon Almeida, Rudini Sampaio
papers.abstract: In 1984, Frank Harary introduced the first convexity games in graphs, all of them based on the geodesic convexity, which is the graph convexity related to shortest paths. In 2024, Ara\'ujo et al. obtained the first PSPACE-hardness proofs on some of these geodesic games and generalized them to any graph convexity. In this paper, we investigate convexity games on several known induced path convexities: the monophonic $\mathrm{m}$-convexity and the $\ell_k$-convexities, based on induced paths and on induced paths of size at most $k$. We prove that the hull games $\mathrm{CHG}_{\mathrm{m}}$, $\mathrm{CHG}_{\ell_k}$ and their mis\`ere variants are PSPACE-complete for every $k\ge2$ even in graphs with diameter at most 3. We also use the Sprague-Grundy Theory to obtain a polynomial time algorithm to decide the winner of the games $\mathrm{CHG}_{\mathrm{m}}$ and $\mathrm{CHG}_{\ell_k}$ for any $k\ge2$ in disjoint unions of paths and cycles. For $k\ge3$ odd, we prove that Alice (1st player) wins $\mathrm{CHG}_{\ell_k}$ in the path $P_n$ if and only if $n$ is odd and she wins in the cycle $C_n$ if and only if $n=3$ or $n=\alpha\cdot (k+1)-1$ with $\alpha\ge2$. For $k\ge2$ even, the only periodic nimber sequences of $\mathrm{CHG}_{\ell_k}$ obtained through extensive computational testing occurred for $k=2^h-4$ with $h\ge3$, e.g, $k\in\{4,12,28,60,\ldots\}$. In this case ($k=2^h-4$ with $h\ge3$), we prove that the nimber sequences of $\mathrm{CHG}_{\ell_k}$ in $P_n$ and in $C_n$ are periodic and Alice loses (resp. wins) in $P_n$ (resp. $C_n$) with $n>k$ only when $n=3k+4$ (resp. $n\in\{2k+1,5k+3\}$). Finally, we show that, for $k=2$, the game $\mathrm{CHG}_{\ell_2}$ in paths $P_n$ is closely related to the classical game Couples-are-Forever of J. H. Conway: it is still an open problem if the nimber sequence is periodic or not and Alice loses only for 12 values of $n$ up to $100$ million.

papers.title: Spectral theory for dynamical large deviations in non-Markov self-interacting processes
papers.abstract: We develop a spectral theory for dynamical large deviations in non-Markov jump processes and non-Markov chains, whose dynamics depends on the past through state- and jump-dependent empirical observables. We demonstrate that a multiscale Wentzel-Kramers-Brillouin-Jeffreys (WKBJ) Ansatz separates fast configurational relaxation from slow memory evolution, reducing the Feynman--Kac equation for occupation and flux statistics to an eigenvalue problem for a new tilted operator coupled to Hamilton--Jacobi characteristics. This provides a computationally efficient framework for quantifying fluctuations in a broad class of non-Markovian systems. We illustrate our general results with a bistable self-induced East model.

papers.title: Spectral Analysis Beyond the Spectral Gap: Rapid Mixing of Quantum Gibbs Samplers in One Dimension
papers.abstract: We prove rapid mixing of a quantum Gibbs sampler for general one-dimensional non-commuting local spin systems at every fixed positive temperature. In particular, for a system of $n$ sites, we show that the Kubo--Martin--Schwinger (KMS) detailed-balanced Gibbs sampler of~\cite{CKG2023} converges from any initial state to trace-norm error $\epsilon$ in time $O(\log^4(n)+\log(1/\epsilon))$. This improves the previous $O(n+\log(1/\epsilon))$ bound and establishes rapid mixing beyond high-temperature and weak-interaction regimes. Our proof explains why the slowest decay rate, captured by the spectral gap, can substantially underestimate the speed of equilibration. The key insight is that a state far from equilibrium must have a substantial component outside the span of low-weight Pauli operators, where stronger dissipation estimates apply. This yields two stages of relaxation: a double-exponential convergence from a bad initial state, followed by exponential convergence near equilibrium. We turn this mechanism into a framework for proving rapid mixing through spectral analysis beyond the gap. Our decay estimate is equivalent to exponential convergence in sandwiched R\'enyi-2 divergence. Together with the spectral gap, it also implies a modified logarithmic Sobolev inequality with rate $\Omega(\log^{-4}(n))$.

papers.title: Classification of bipartite observables II: NIP observables and the Todorcevic trichotomy
papers.abstract: This is the second of a series of three papers that bring model theory to quantum information. The dividing lines of Shelah's classification theory, which separate the tame first-order theories from the wild ones, become properties of bipartite observables: properties of the expectation values obtained when two independently prepared quantum systems are idealized one after the other. In this paper we focus on Shelah's independence property. An observable without it has idealized responses of the first Baire class, and Todor\v{c}evi\'c's trichotomy for Rosenthal compacta divides such observables into three classes, each containing a physical order. In the transverse-field Ising model, the spontaneous magnetization decides whether the family of magnetizations is stable or lies in the second class.

papers.title: A first order nonabelian antisymmetric tensor model with hidden higher symmetry
papers.abstract: We present a nonabelian complex self-dual antisymmetric tensor model, with gauged internal symmetry, comprising a complex multiplet of massless self-dual antisymmetric tensor fields and its conjugate (interacting with massless Yang-Mills gauge fields). We build the model at the classical level, via a first order formulation, assigning local fields to a component expansion over the Dirac algebra and a basis of internal matrices, with Lorentz and gauge invariance ensured by tracing, and applying an appropriate bilinear form. The full expansion requires auxiliary place-holder fields, which are not potentials, but become curvatures (field strengths) after elimination via their algebraic equations of motion. The component expansion over the Dirac algebra is closed under multiplication by additional internal matrices, which are not gauge group generators, but mix internal components, and link auxiliary curvatures with potentials. The model is shown to be invariant under such transformations, and thus possesses a type of hidden internal symmetry. We analyze the specific case of gauge group $SU(2)\! \times \! U(1)$, and as higher symmetry candidates, we consider both the Lie group $SU(3)$ and the Lie superalgebra $SU(2/1)$ (with the additional matrices acting via Lie brackets, or graded Lie brackets, respectively).

papers.title: Finite-time quantum equilibration from local correlations
papers.abstract: An isolated quantum system evolves reversibly, yet a small subsystem can lose nearly all information about its initial state. Conserved quantities may retain some of this information, depending on how strongly they overlap with local observables. Here we consider a subsystem in an arbitrary initial state coupled to a maximally mixed bath. We show that the worst-input mean-square equilibration error, maximised over window origins, is bounded from above and below by the mean square of a complete local autocorrelation, with the stationary part subtracted. The two mean-square quantities are linearly comparable. A correlation record over a finite interval therefore controls the equilibration error in every interval of the same length, and the result extends to nonnegative observation weights with nonnegative Fourier transform. The result allows arbitrary degeneracies of energies and gaps. We apply it to two static Hamiltonian families. For fixed spin subsystems in the one-particle sector of a bounded-range periodic clock, fixed-accuracy thermalisation is guaranteed on windows that grow only slightly faster than linearly with system size, despite exponentially small positive energies. A random commuting model with logarithmic interaction range retains an extensive set of conserved observables. Its expected mean-square error is bounded by a finite-size term and an inverse-time term. The inverse-time dependence is unavoidable because of the initial transient. These examples show how local relaxation can coexist with exact conservation laws and a finely spaced spectrum.

papers.title: GROMM: Generative Risk-neutral Option Market Models
papers.authors: Magnus Wiese, Hans Buehler, Blanka Horvath
papers.abstract: We present a statically and dynamically arbitrage-free European option market model with smooth interpolation between option prices, based on the SANOS framework, and prove that its dynamics admit a unique strong solution. In spirit, it is a stochastic model for local volatility when the latter is used as a representation of a European option price surface, not as a pricing model. We illustrate the strength of our approach on S&P Index Option data from January 2022 to August 2025. We show that the model's initial state fits within bid/ask for more than 95% of relevant market option prices. We then train the model dynamics under $\mathbb{P}$ and $\mathbb{Q}$ and show that the model is indeed free of arbitrage while fitting the dynamics of the market well. We also propose a range of BHW-tests to test for absence of arbitrage.

papers.title: Self-organizing reinforcement learning: a learner-free swarm approaches the explore-exploit optimum
papers.abstract: The explore/exploit trade-off is the core problem of reinforcement learning (RL). We show that a minimal foraging swarm approaches its optimum - the ideal-free / Nash allocation of a multi-agent resource-sharing game (an equilibrium, not a return maximum) - with no learner and no reward signal. Agents explore by heavy-tailed (Levy) flights, recruit neighbours to a discovery through a threshold cascade on their proximity network, and disperse as a patch crowds; this cascade cycle balances exploration and exploitation and drives foragers toward the ideal free distribution. The swarm attains the shape of this optimum (committed foragers track richness with slope 0.94) but not its exact equilibrium - it stays measurably exploitable - reaching it dynamically (~150 steps) through the coupling of recruitment to movement: remove the coupling and matching collapses (0.94 -> 0.08). The RL sits at the level of the problem and the allocation reached, not the micro-rule: no step evaluates payoff (reward-free by construction, though the crowd signal is informationally tied to payoff), and the swarm reaches the allocation without learning it (quality plateaus and re-settles after resources move, no cumulative gain). Against a trained baseline the comparison is two-sided: in an easier, disembodied game a learner is more precise, while in the same embodied environment the reward-free swarm reaches ~65% of a validated oracle ceiling at zero training and leads until trained PPO and centralised-critic (CTDE) learners overtake it (~74-75%, 16 seeds, all above the swarm mean) after ~4,000 of 15,000 training steps - its advantage is in budget, not asymptote. In this one setting we read it not as beating RL but as a strong zero-shot, reward-free operating point: a demonstration that the self-organizing physics of a minimal swarm can carry a collective close to the optimum RL seeks, with none of RL's machinery.

papers.title: Union of Translates of a Convex Body
papers.abstract: Let $K\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ be a strictly convex body and let $Z\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ be a finite set of sites in general position. We consider the problem of calculating the volume $\mu_d$ of $\bigcup_{z\in Z}(z-K)$. Let $V_z$ be the Voronoi cell of $z\in Z$ with respect to the convex distance function induced by $K$, and let $N$ be the nerve of the Voronoi cells. When $K$ is a ball, a classical result reduces the inclusion-exclusion formula to a sum over $N$: $\mu_d(\bigcup_{z\in Z}(z-K))=\sum_{J\in N}(-1)^{|J|+1}\mu_d(\bigcap_{z\in J}(z-K))$. When may the hypothesis that $K$ is a ball be dropped? We show that for $d\leq 2$ the reduced formula holds for every strictly convex $K$, while for each $d\geq 3$ there is a strictly convex $K$ for which it fails. For $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$, let $\chi_x$ be the Euler characteristic of the subcomplex of $N$ induced by the sites lying in $K+x$. A sufficient condition for the reduced formula to hold is $\chi_x\equiv 1$ on the union. When $d=3$ and $K$ is $C^4$, we show that $\chi_x\equiv 1$ on the union for all $Z$ in general position if and only if $K$ is an ellipsoid. The proof relies on the Fubini-Pick affine invariant.

papers.title: Automatic Differentiation with Constraints in Forward and Inverse Problems
papers.authors: Nikolay Yavich, Alexander Ryabov, Viacheslav Naumov, Sayan Ranu, N. M. Anoop Krishnan, Evgeny Burnaev, Vladimir Vanovskiy
papers.abstract: Approximate solutions of partial differential equations (PDEs) on unstructured grids can be represented on a graph. Numerical optimization involving stiff evolutionary and static PDEs often requires solving a large system of equations, which can be treated as a constraint. In this work, we present a fully differentiable graph-based implicit solver that incorporates this constraint. We evaluate its performance across four key tasks: a) linear and nonlinear forward modeling of evolutionary and static problems, b) solving inverse problems to estimate equation coefficients, c) solving inverse problems to estimate the right-hand side, and d) learnable graph coarsening to accelerate forward modeling. The stability and differentiability of our solver enable significant reductions in the complexity of forward modeling while efficiently addressing related inverse problems. These capabilities make it a powerful tool for different physics and engineering applications, in particular for geophysics, where inverse problems are commonly solved in order to reduce the model uncertainty.
